Question:
Find all actors from Canada who acted in " James Bond " movies
ground_truth.answer: SELECT t1.name FROM CAST AS t2 JOIN actor AS t1 ON t2.aid  =  t1.aid JOIN movie AS t3 ON t3.mid  =  t2.msid WHERE t1.nationality  =  "Canada" AND t3.title  =  "James Bond";

prefix_hints.sol_2: I then join the corresponding movie through the cast record’s `msid`, which matches the movie id: `FROM CAST AS t2 JOIN actor AS t1 ON t2.aid  =  t1.aid JOIN movie AS t3 ON t3.mid  =  t2.msid`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I restrict the actors to those whose nationality is Canada: `FROM CAST AS t2 JOIN actor AS t1 ON t2.aid  =  t1.aid JOIN movie AS t3 ON t3.mid  =  t2.msid WHERE t1.nationality  =  "Canada"`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I further restrict the joined movies to the title James Bond: `FROM CAST AS t2 JOIN actor AS t1 ON t2.aid  =  t1.aid JOIN movie AS t3 ON t3.mid  =  t2.msid WHERE t1.nationality  =  "Canada" AND t3.title  =  "James Bond"`.

What is the GDP for Service of the country with Fuenlabrada as its city.
ground_truth.answer: SELECT T4.Service * T4.GDP FROM country AS T1 INNER JOIN province AS T2 ON T1.Code = T2.Country INNER JOIN city AS T3 ON T3.Province = T2.Name INNER JOIN economy AS T4 ON T4.Country = T2.Country WHERE T3.Name = 'Fuenlabrada'

prefix_hints.sol_3: I then join the country's economic data using the province country code: `FROM country AS T1 INNER JOIN province AS T2 ON T1.Code = T2.Country INNER JOIN city AS T3 ON T3.Province = T2.Name INNER JOIN economy AS T4 ON T4.Country = T2.Country`.

Question:
Find the number of rooms located on each block floor.
ground_truth.answer: SELECT count(*) ,  T1.blockfloor FROM BLOCK AS T1 JOIN room AS T2 ON T1.blockfloor  =  T2.blockfloor AND T1.blockcode  =  T2.blockcode GROUP BY T1.blockfloor

prefix_hints.sol_2: I join each block to its rooms by matching both the floor and block code: `FROM BLOCK AS T1 JOIN room AS T2 ON T1.blockfloor = T2.blockfloor AND T1.blockcode = T2.blockcode`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I group the matched rooms by block floor to form one result group per floor: `FROM BLOCK AS T1 JOIN room AS T2 ON T1.blockfloor = T2.blockfloor AND T1.blockcode = T2.blockcode GROUP BY T1.blockfloor`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I count the rooms in each group and return the corresponding floor: `SELECT count(*) , T1.blockfloor FROM BLOCK AS T1 JOIN room AS T2 ON T1.blockfloor = T2.blockfloor AND T1.blockcode = T2.blockcode GROUP BY T1.blockfloor`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: This completes the room count for every block floor: `SELECT count(*) ,  T1.blockfloor FROM BLOCK AS T1 JOIN room AS T2 ON T1.blockfloor  =  T2.blockfloor AND T1.blockcode  =  T2.blockcode GROUP BY T1.blockfloor`.

prefix_hints.sol_3: I link each student in that second query to their recorded pets through `has_pet`: `SELECT stuid FROM student EXCEPT SELECT T1.stuid FROM student AS T1 JOIN has_pet AS T2 ON T1.stuid  =  T2.stuid`.

ground_truth.answer: SELECT T2.Class FROM ProductReview AS T1 INNER JOIN Product AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID GROUP BY T2.Class ORDER BY COUNT(T1.ProductReviewID) DESC LIMIT 1

ground_truth.answer: SELECT T2.coachID, T1.nameNick FROM Master AS T1 INNER JOIN Coaches AS T2 ON T1.coachID = T2.coachID WHERE T2.year = 2009 ORDER BY CAST(T2.W AS REAL) / (T2.W + T2.L) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start with `Master`, which contains each coach's nickname: `FROM Master AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join the coaching records by coach ID so I can associate each nickname with season wins and losses: `FROM Master AS T1 INNER JOIN Coaches AS T2 ON T1.coachID = T2.coachID`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I restrict the coaching records to the 2009 season: `FROM Master AS T1 INNER JOIN Coaches AS T2 ON T1.coachID = T2.coachID WHERE T2.year = 2009`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I rank the coaches by wins divided by total wins and losses, casting wins to REAL for decimal division: `FROM Master AS T1 INNER JOIN Coaches AS T2 ON T1.coachID = T2.coachID WHERE T2.year = 2009 ORDER BY CAST(T2.W AS REAL) / (T2.W + T2.L) DESC`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I return the top-ranked coach's ID and nickname by limiting the ordered results to one row: `SELECT T2.coachID, T1.nameNick FROM Master AS T1 INNER JOIN Coaches AS T2 ON T1.coachID = T2.coachID WHERE T2.year = 2009 ORDER BY CAST(T2.W AS REAL) / (T2.W + T2.L) DESC LIMIT 1`.

Question:
Among the products from the mountain product line, how many of them are sold by over 2 vendors?

Evidence:
mountain product line refers to ProductLine = 'M'; sold by over 5 vendors refers to count(Name)>5
ground_truth.answer: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN T1.ProductLine = 'M' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM Product AS T1 INNER JOIN ProductVendor AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID INNER JOIN Vendor AS T3 ON T2.BusinessEntityID = T3.BusinessEntityID GROUP BY T1.ProductID HAVING COUNT(T1.Name) > 2

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start with products and link each one to its vendor relationships through the shared product id: `FROM Product AS T1 INNER JOIN ProductVendor AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join the corresponding vendor records through the vendor business entity id: `FROM Product AS T1 INNER JOIN ProductVendor AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID INNER JOIN Vendor AS T3 ON T2.BusinessEntityID = T3.BusinessEntityID`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I group the joined rows by product so each group represents the vendors associated with one product: `FROM Product AS T1 INNER JOIN ProductVendor AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID INNER JOIN Vendor AS T3 ON T2.BusinessEntityID = T3.BusinessEntityID GROUP BY T1.ProductID`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I retain product groups with more than two joined vendor rows by counting the product name occurrences: `FROM Product AS T1 INNER JOIN ProductVendor AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID INNER JOIN Vendor AS T3 ON T2.BusinessEntityID = T3.BusinessEntityID GROUP BY T1.ProductID HAVING COUNT(T1.Name) > 2`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I finish by conditionally summing the qualifying rows whose product line is mountain, represented by `ProductLine = 'M'`: `SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN T1.ProductLine = 'M' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM Product AS T1 INNER JOIN ProductVendor AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID INNER JOIN Vendor AS T3 ON T2.BusinessEntityID = T3.BusinessEntityID GROUP BY T1.ProductID HAVING COUNT(T1.Name) > 2`.

ground_truth.answer: SELECT T2.name ,  T1.team_id_winner FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T1.year  =  2008 GROUP BY T1.team_id_winner ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1;

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start with postseason results and join each winning team id to the team record that provides its name: `FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner  =  T2.team_id_br`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I restrict the postseason results to 2008: `FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T1.year  =  2008`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I group the results by winning team so each team's postseason wins can be counted: `FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T1.year  =  2008 GROUP BY T1.team_id_winner`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I order the teams by their result count in descending order and retain the top one: `FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T1.year  =  2008 GROUP BY T1.team_id_winner ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I project that team's name and winning-team id, completing the query: `SELECT T2.name ,  T1.team_id_winner FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T1.year  =  2008 GROUP BY T1.team_id_winner ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1;`.

How many employees do not have any suffix and what are their organization level?

Do not have any suffix means Suffix is null

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start with the employee records so each qualifying employee is identified by `BusinessEntityID`: `FROM Employee AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join each employee to the corresponding person record, where the suffix is stored: `FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN Person AS T2 USING (BusinessEntityID)`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I keep employees whose person record has a null suffix: `FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN Person AS T2 USING (BusinessEntityID) WHERE T2.Suffix IS NULL`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I select and group by employee identifier so the inner result contains one row per qualifying employee: `SELECT T1.BusinessEntityID FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN Person AS T2 USING (BusinessEntityID) WHERE T2.Suffix IS NULL GROUP BY T1.BusinessEntityID`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I wrap that employee-level result as `T3` and count its identifiers: `SELECT COUNT(T3.BusinessEntityID) FROM ( SELECT T1.BusinessEntityID FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN Person AS T2 USING (BusinessEntityID) WHERE T2.Suffix IS NULL GROUP BY T1.BusinessEntityID ) AS T3`.

ground_truth.answer: SELECT DISTINCT T1.customer_name FROM customers AS T1 JOIN customer_orders AS T2 ON T1.customer_id  =  T2.customer_id JOIN order_items AS T3 ON T2.order_id  =  T3.order_id GROUP BY T1.customer_id HAVING COUNT (DISTINCT T3.product_id)  >=  3

prefix_hints.sol_1: I begin with customers and link each one to their orders through the customer id: `FROM customers AS T1 JOIN customer_orders AS T2 ON T1.customer_id  =  T2.customer_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I then join each order to its items so I can identify the products each customer purchased: `FROM customers AS T1 JOIN customer_orders AS T2 ON T1.customer_id  =  T2.customer_id JOIN order_items AS T3 ON T2.order_id  =  T3.order_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I group the joined records by customer so the purchased products can be counted for each customer: `FROM customers AS T1 JOIN customer_orders AS T2 ON T1.customer_id  =  T2.customer_id JOIN order_items AS T3 ON T2.order_id  =  T3.order_id GROUP BY T1.customer_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I retain customers whose count of distinct purchased product ids is at least three: `FROM customers AS T1 JOIN customer_orders AS T2 ON T1.customer_id  =  T2.customer_id JOIN order_items AS T3 ON T2.order_id  =  T3.order_id GROUP BY T1.customer_id HAVING COUNT (DISTINCT T3.product_id)  >=  3`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I return the distinct names of those qualifying customers: `SELECT DISTINCT T1.customer_name FROM customers AS T1 JOIN customer_orders AS T2 ON T1.customer_id  =  T2.customer_id JOIN order_items AS T3 ON T2.order_id  =  T3.order_id GROUP BY T1.customer_id HAVING COUNT (DISTINCT T3.product_id)  >=  3`.

Question:
What is the job title of the oldest employee in the company? In which department is he in?

Evidence:
oldest employee refers to min(BirthDate)
ground_truth.answer: SELECT T2.JobTitle, T4.Name FROM Person AS T1 INNER JOIN Employee AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID INNER JOIN EmployeeDepartmentHistory AS T3 ON T2.BusinessEntityID = T3.BusinessEntityID INNER JOIN Department AS T4 ON T3.DepartmentID = T4.DepartmentID ORDER BY T2.HireDate LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start with each person’s employee record so the employee’s job information is available: `FROM Person AS T1 INNER JOIN Employee AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I connect the employee to their department history through the shared business entity id: `FROM Person AS T1 INNER JOIN Employee AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID INNER JOIN EmployeeDepartmentHistory AS T3 ON T2.BusinessEntityID = T3.BusinessEntityID`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I then join the department record to obtain its name: `FROM Person AS T1 INNER JOIN Employee AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID INNER JOIN EmployeeDepartmentHistory AS T3 ON T2.BusinessEntityID = T3.BusinessEntityID INNER JOIN Department AS T4 ON T3.DepartmentID = T4.DepartmentID`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I order the joined records by hire date and retain the earliest one: `FROM Person AS T1 INNER JOIN Employee AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID INNER JOIN EmployeeDepartmentHistory AS T3 ON T2.BusinessEntityID = T3.BusinessEntityID INNER JOIN Department AS T4 ON T3.DepartmentID = T4.DepartmentID ORDER BY T2.HireDate LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I return that employee’s job title and department name: `SELECT T2.JobTitle, T4.Name FROM Person AS T1 INNER JOIN Employee AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID INNER JOIN EmployeeDepartmentHistory AS T3 ON T2.BusinessEntityID = T3.BusinessEntityID INNER JOIN Department AS T4 ON T3.DepartmentID = T4.DepartmentID ORDER BY T2.HireDate LIMIT 1`.

prefix_hints.sol_3: I sort representatives by year-to-date sales in descending order so the highest value comes first: `FROM SalesPerson AS T1 INNER JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID ORDER BY T1.SalesYTD DESC`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I retain only that top-ranked representative: `FROM SalesPerson AS T1 INNER JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID ORDER BY T1.SalesYTD DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I return the representative's first, middle, and last names: `SELECT T2.FirstName, T2.MiddleName, T2.LastName FROM SalesPerson AS T1 INNER JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID ORDER BY T1.SalesYTD DESC LIMIT 1`.

Question:
Show the names of customers who have the most mailshots.
ground_truth.answer: SELECT T2.customer_name FROM mailshot_customers AS T1 JOIN customers AS T2 ON T1.customer_id  =  T2.customer_id GROUP BY T1.customer_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start from the mailshot-customer records, since each row represents a mailshot associated with a customer: `FROM mailshot_customers AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join customers on the shared customer id so the corresponding customer name is available: `FROM mailshot_customers AS T1 JOIN customers AS T2 ON T1.customer_id  =  T2.customer_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I group the records by customer so each customer's mailshots can be counted together: `FROM mailshot_customers AS T1 JOIN customers AS T2 ON T1.customer_id  =  T2.customer_id GROUP BY T1.customer_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I order the customer groups by their mailshot counts in descending order and keep the highest one: `FROM mailshot_customers AS T1 JOIN customers AS T2 ON T1.customer_id  =  T2.customer_id GROUP BY T1.customer_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I project the name of the customer in that highest-count group: `SELECT T2.customer_name FROM mailshot_customers AS T1 JOIN customers AS T2 ON T1.customer_id  =  T2.customer_id GROUP BY T1.customer_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1`.

in 1990 refers to year = 1990; winning rate of more than 75% refers to Divide(won, games) > 0.75

prefix_hints.sol_2: I join each record to the matching team using both the team id and year so the season-level wins and games are available: `FROM players_teams AS T1 INNER JOIN teams AS T2 ON T1.tmID = T2.tmID AND T1.year = T2.year`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I retain teams whose winning percentage is greater than 75, casting wins and games to REAL for the division: `FROM players_teams AS T1 INNER JOIN teams AS T2 ON T1.tmID = T2.tmID AND T1.year = T2.year WHERE CAST(T2.won AS REAL) * 100 / CAST(T2.games AS REAL) > 75`.

Question:
Which product gets the most reviews?

Evidence:
most reviews refers to MAX(count(ProductID))
ground_truth.answer: SELECT T2.Name FROM ProductReview AS T1 INNER JOIN Product AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID GROUP BY T1.ProductID ORDER BY COUNT(T1.ProductReviewID) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start with `ProductReview`, where each row represents a review and identifies its product: `FROM ProductReview AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join `Product` on the product id so I can return the reviewed product's name: `FROM ProductReview AS T1 INNER JOIN Product AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I group the review rows by product to calculate a review count for each one: `FROM ProductReview AS T1 INNER JOIN Product AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID GROUP BY T1.ProductID`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I sort the products by their review counts in descending order and keep the top result: `FROM ProductReview AS T1 INNER JOIN Product AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID GROUP BY T1.ProductID ORDER BY COUNT(T1.ProductReviewID) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I project the name of that most-reviewed product: `SELECT T2.Name FROM ProductReview AS T1 INNER JOIN Product AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID GROUP BY T1.ProductID ORDER BY COUNT(T1.ProductReviewID) DESC LIMIT 1`.

Question:
Who is the Lutheran representative that served in the state of Ohio for 14 years before becoming a senator?

Evidence:
Lutheran refers to religion_bio = 'Lutheran'; representative refers to type = 'rep'; served for 14 years refers to SUBTRACT(SUM(CAST(strftime('%Y', end)), CAST(strftime('%Y', start)))) = 14;
ground_truth.answer: SELECT CASE WHEN SUM(CAST(strftime('%Y', T2.end) AS int) - CAST(strftime('%Y', T2.start) AS int)) = 14 THEN official_full_name END FROM current AS T1 INNER JOIN `current-terms` AS T2 ON T1.bioguide_id = T2.bioguide WHERE T1.religion_bio = 'Lutheran' AND T2.state = 'OH' AND T2.type = 'rep'

prefix_hints.sol_1: I link each current legislator to their terms using the bioguide identifier: `FROM current AS T1 INNER JOIN `current-terms` AS T2 ON T1.bioguide_id = T2.bioguide`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I narrow the joined records to Lutheran legislators who served in Ohio: `FROM current AS T1 INNER JOIN `current-terms` AS T2 ON T1.bioguide_id = T2.bioguide WHERE T1.religion_bio = 'Lutheran' AND T2.state = 'OH'`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I further restrict the terms to service as a representative: `FROM current AS T1 INNER JOIN `current-terms` AS T2 ON T1.bioguide_id = T2.bioguide WHERE T1.religion_bio = 'Lutheran' AND T2.state = 'OH' AND T2.type = 'rep'`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I sum the differences between each term's end and start years, returning the legislator's official name when that service totals 14 years: `SELECT CASE WHEN SUM(CAST(strftime('%Y', T2.end) AS int) - CAST(strftime('%Y', T2.start) AS int)) = 14 THEN official_full_name END FROM current AS T1 INNER JOIN `current-terms` AS T2 ON T1.bioguide_id = T2.bioguide WHERE T1.religion_bio = 'Lutheran' AND T2.state = 'OH' AND T2.type = 'rep'`.

prefix_hints.sol_3: I then join `Vendor` through the relationship's `BusinessEntityID` to obtain vendor names: `FROM Product AS T1 INNER JOIN ProductVendor AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID INNER JOIN ProductSubcategory AS T3 ON T1.ProductSubcategoryID = T3.ProductSubcategoryID INNER JOIN Vendor AS T4 ON T2.BusinessEntityID = T4.BusinessEntityID`.

prefix_hints.sol_3: I further keep only players whose overall rating was 77: `FROM Player AS t1 INNER JOIN Player_Attributes AS t2 ON t1.player_api_id = t2.player_api_id WHERE SUBSTR(t2.`date`, 1, 10) = '2016-06-23' AND t2.overall_rating = 77`.

Question:
What is the average number of territories do each sales representative is in charge of?

Evidence:
sales representative refers to Title = 'Sales Representative'; average number of territories = divide(count(TerritoryID) , count(EmployeeID)) where Title = 'Sales Representative'
ground_truth.answer: SELECT CAST(COUNT(T2.TerritoryID) AS REAL) / COUNT(DISTINCT T1.EmployeeID) FROM Employees AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeeTerritories AS T2 ON T1.EmployeeID = T2.EmployeeID WHERE T1.Title = 'Sales Representative'

prefix_hints.sol_4: I divide the territory count by the number of distinct sales representatives so employees with multiple territories are counted once in the denominator: `SELECT CAST(COUNT(T2.TerritoryID) AS REAL) / COUNT(DISTINCT T1.EmployeeID) FROM Employees AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeeTerritories AS T2 ON T1.EmployeeID = T2.EmployeeID WHERE T1.Title = 'Sales Representative'`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: This gives the requested average number of territories per sales representative: `SELECT CAST(COUNT(T2.TerritoryID) AS REAL) / COUNT(DISTINCT T1.EmployeeID) FROM Employees AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeeTerritories AS T2 ON T1.EmployeeID = T2.EmployeeID WHERE T1.Title = 'Sales Representative'`.

prefix_hints.sol_2: I restrict this first owner set to programs broadcast in the morning: `SELECT t1.owner FROM program AS t1 JOIN broadcast AS t2 ON t1.program_id  =  t2.program_id WHERE t2.Time_of_day  =  "Morning"`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I use INTERSECT so the result will retain owners who also appear in a second set for night programs: `SELECT t1.owner FROM program AS t1 JOIN broadcast AS t2 ON t1.program_id  =  t2.program_id WHERE t2.Time_of_day  =  "Morning" INTERSECT SELECT t1.owner FROM program AS t1`.

prefix_hints.sol_5: I finish the second set by selecting broadcasts at night, leaving exactly the owners represented in both time periods: `SELECT t1.owner FROM program AS t1 JOIN broadcast AS t2 ON t1.program_id  =  t2.program_id WHERE t2.Time_of_day  =  "Morning" INTERSECT SELECT t1.owner FROM program AS t1 JOIN broadcast AS t2 ON t1.program_id  =  t2.program_id WHERE t2.Time_of_day  =  "Night"`.

Question:
What is the company's profit on the product that was rated second-highest by David?

Evidence:
profit on net on a single product = SUBTRACT(ListPrice, StandardCost); second highest rating refers to Rating = 4; David is the ReviewerName;
ground_truth.answer: SELECT T2.ListPrice - T2.StandardCost FROM ProductReview AS T1 INNER JOIN Product AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID WHERE T1.ReviewerName = 'David' ORDER BY T1.Rating DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.sol_1: David's ratings are in `ProductReview`, while the product pricing and cost are in `Product`, so I join them by product id: `FROM ProductReview AS T1 INNER JOIN Product AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I restrict the reviews to those submitted by David: `FROM ProductReview AS T1 INNER JOIN Product AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID WHERE T1.ReviewerName = 'David'`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I sort David's reviews from highest rating downward to identify the requested ranked product: `FROM ProductReview AS T1 INNER JOIN Product AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID WHERE T1.ReviewerName = 'David' ORDER BY T1.Rating DESC`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I keep the first product from that descending rating order: `FROM ProductReview AS T1 INNER JOIN Product AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID WHERE T1.ReviewerName = 'David' ORDER BY T1.Rating DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I calculate the product's profit by subtracting its standard cost from its list price: `SELECT T2.ListPrice - T2.StandardCost FROM ProductReview AS T1 INNER JOIN Product AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID WHERE T1.ReviewerName = 'David' ORDER BY T1.Rating DESC LIMIT 1`.

prefix_hints.sol_2: I join each salary record to its player so I can identify the earner by name: `FROM salary AS T1 JOIN player AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I identify Len Barker by matching both his first and last names: `FROM salary AS T1 JOIN player AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id WHERE T2.name_first  =  'Len' AND T2.name_last = 'Barker'`.

Question:
What is the highest pay rate of the employees who are exempt from collective bargaining?

Evidence:
employee exempt from collective bargaining refers to SalariedFlag = 1; highest pay rate refers to max(Rate)
ground_truth.answer: SELECT T1.Rate FROM EmployeePayHistory AS T1 INNER JOIN Employee AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T2.SalariedFlag = 1 ORDER BY T1.Rate DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start with the employee pay history and select each recorded pay rate: `SELECT T1.Rate FROM EmployeePayHistory AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join each pay record to its employee through the shared business entity id: `SELECT T1.Rate FROM EmployeePayHistory AS T1 INNER JOIN Employee AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I keep employees marked as exempt from collective bargaining by `SalariedFlag = 1`: `SELECT T1.Rate FROM EmployeePayHistory AS T1 INNER JOIN Employee AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T2.SalariedFlag = 1`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I sort the qualifying pay rates from highest to lowest: `SELECT T1.Rate FROM EmployeePayHistory AS T1 INNER JOIN Employee AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T2.SalariedFlag = 1 ORDER BY T1.Rate DESC`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I take the first sorted row to return the single highest pay rate: `SELECT T1.Rate FROM EmployeePayHistory AS T1 INNER JOIN Employee AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T2.SalariedFlag = 1 ORDER BY T1.Rate DESC LIMIT 1`.

brand of root beer refers to BrandName; produced by Dr Pepper Snapple Group refers to BreweryName = 'Dr Pepper Snapple Group'; percentage of purchases = MULTIPLY(DIVIDE(SUM(BrandID WHERE PurchaseDate > = '2014-01-01' AND PurchaseDate < = '2016-12-31'), COUNT(BrandID) WHERE BreweryName = 'Dr Pepper Snapple Group'), 1.0); between 2014 to 2016 refers to PurchaseDate > = '2014-01-01' AND PurchaseDate < = '2016-12-31;
ground_truth.answer: SELECT T1.BrandName , CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T2.PurchaseDate >= '2014-01-01' AND T2.PurchaseDate <= '2016-12-31' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) / COUNT(T2.BrandID) AS purchase FROM rootbeerbrand AS T1 INNER JOIN rootbeer AS T2 ON T1.BrandID = T2.BrandID WHERE T1.BreweryName = 'Dr Pepper Snapple Group' GROUP BY T2.BrandID

Question:
Among the drivers that finished the race in the 2008 Chinese Grand Prix, how many of them have participated in Formula_1 races?

Evidence:
COUNT(raceID) > 0 reveals that this driver participated in races; drivers who finished the race refers to time has value.
ground_truth.answer: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ( SELECT T1.driverId FROM results AS T1 INNER JOIN races AS T2 on T1.raceId = T2.raceId WHERE T2.name = 'Chinese Grand Prix' AND T2.year = 2008 AND T1.time IS NOT NULL GROUP BY T1.driverId HAVING COUNT(T2.raceId) > 0 )

prefix_hints.sol_1: I link each result to its race so I can identify the event and season: `FROM results AS T1 INNER JOIN races AS T2 on T1.raceId = T2.raceId`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I restrict the rows to the 2008 Chinese Grand Prix and treat a non-null result time as evidence that the driver finished: `FROM results AS T1 INNER JOIN races AS T2 on T1.raceId = T2.raceId WHERE T2.name = 'Chinese Grand Prix' AND T2.year = 2008 AND T1.time IS NOT NULL`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I group these result rows by driver and retain drivers whose race count confirms participation: `FROM results AS T1 INNER JOIN races AS T2 on T1.raceId = T2.raceId WHERE T2.name = 'Chinese Grand Prix' AND T2.year = 2008 AND T1.time IS NOT NULL GROUP BY T1.driverId HAVING COUNT(T2.raceId) > 0`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I select each qualifying driver id to form the derived set that will be counted: `SELECT T1.driverId FROM results AS T1 INNER JOIN races AS T2 on T1.raceId = T2.raceId WHERE T2.name = 'Chinese Grand Prix' AND T2.year = 2008 AND T1.time IS NOT NULL GROUP BY T1.driverId HAVING COUNT(T2.raceId) > 0`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I wrap that driver set and count its rows to obtain the requested number of drivers: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ( SELECT T1.driverId FROM results AS T1 INNER JOIN races AS T2 on T1.raceId = T2.raceId WHERE T2.name = 'Chinese Grand Prix' AND T2.year = 2008 AND T1.time IS NOT NULL GROUP BY T1.driverId HAVING COUNT(T2.raceId) > 0 )`.

Question:
Which federal republic country in Europe has the most provinces, and what proportion of GDP is devoted to services?
Calculate the population density as well.

Evidence:
Republic is on of government forms; Percentage of Services of the GDP was mentioned in economy.Service; Population Density = Population / Area
ground_truth.answer: SELECT T1.Country, T2.Service , SUM(T1.Population) / SUM(T1.Area) FROM province AS T1 INNER JOIN economy AS T2 ON T1.Country = T2.Country WHERE T1.Country IN ( SELECT Country FROM encompasses WHERE Continent = 'Europe' ) GROUP BY T1.Country, T2.Service ORDER BY COUNT(T1.Name) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start from `province`, since its rows let me count provinces by country and sum their population and area: `FROM province AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join `economy` on the country code so the service share of GDP is available for each country: `FROM province AS T1 INNER JOIN economy AS T2 ON T1.Country = T2.Country`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I restrict the countries to those encompassed by Europe using the continent mapping subquery: `FROM province AS T1 INNER JOIN economy AS T2 ON T1.Country = T2.Country WHERE T1.Country IN ( SELECT Country FROM encompasses WHERE Continent = 'Europe' )`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I group the province rows by country and service share, then return the country, its service proportion, and population density calculated from the summed population and area: `SELECT T1.Country, T2.Service , SUM(T1.Population) / SUM(T1.Area) FROM province AS T1 INNER JOIN economy AS T2 ON T1.Country = T2.Country WHERE T1.Country IN ( SELECT Country FROM encompasses WHERE Continent = 'Europe' ) GROUP BY T1.Country, T2.Service`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I order the country groups by their province counts in descending order and keep the top one: `SELECT T1.Country, T2.Service , SUM(T1.Population) / SUM(T1.Area) FROM province AS T1 INNER JOIN economy AS T2 ON T1.Country = T2.Country WHERE T1.Country IN ( SELECT Country FROM encompasses WHERE Continent = 'Europe' ) GROUP BY T1.Country, T2.Service ORDER BY COUNT(T1.Name) DESC LIMIT 1`.

prefix_hints.sol_2: I join each business to its reviews so the funny-vote classification is available: `FROM Business AS T1 INNER JOIN Reviews AS T2 ON T1.business_id = T2.business_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I restrict the joined businesses to Phoenix: `FROM Business AS T1 INNER JOIN Reviews AS T2 ON T1.business_id = T2.business_id WHERE T1.city = 'Phoenix'`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I count low funny-vote rows conditionally, cast that count to REAL, multiply by 100, and divide by the total business count: `SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T2.review_votes_funny = 'Low' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(T1.business_id) FROM Business AS T1 INNER JOIN Reviews AS T2 ON T1.business_id = T2.business_id WHERE T1.city = 'Phoenix'`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: This completes the percentage calculation for Phoenix businesses: `SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T2.review_votes_funny = 'Low' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(T1.business_id) FROM Business AS T1 INNER JOIN Reviews AS T2 ON T1.business_id = T2.business_id WHERE T1.city = 'Phoenix'`.

prefix_hints.sol_3: I keep transactions whose quantity exceeds 10,000 pieces: `FROM Product AS T1 INNER JOIN TransactionHistory AS T2 ON T1.ProductID = T2.ProductID WHERE T2.Quantity > 10000`.

Question:
What is the name, address, and number of students in the departments that have the 3 most students?
ground_truth.answer: SELECT T2.dept_name ,  T2.dept_address ,  count(*) FROM student AS T1 JOIN department AS T2 ON T1.dept_code  =  T2.dept_code GROUP BY T1.dept_code ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 3

prefix_hints.sol_1: I join each student to the corresponding department so I can associate department details with student records: `FROM student AS T1 JOIN department AS T2 ON T1.dept_code = T2.dept_code`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I group the joined records by department so each group can provide its student count: `FROM student AS T1 JOIN department AS T2 ON T1.dept_code = T2.dept_code GROUP BY T1.dept_code`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I order the department groups by their student counts from highest to lowest: `FROM student AS T1 JOIN department AS T2 ON T1.dept_code = T2.dept_code GROUP BY T1.dept_code ORDER BY count(*) DESC`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I retain the first three groups to get the departments with the most students: `FROM student AS T1 JOIN department AS T2 ON T1.dept_code = T2.dept_code GROUP BY T1.dept_code ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 3`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I project each qualifying department's name, address, and student count, completing the query: `SELECT T2.dept_name ,  T2.dept_address ,  count(*) FROM student AS T1 JOIN department AS T2 ON T1.dept_code  =  T2.dept_code GROUP BY T1.dept_code ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 3`.

Question:
Give the full names of the countries that are located in more than one continent.
ground_truth.answer: SELECT T3.Name FROM continent AS T1 INNER JOIN encompasses AS T2 ON T1.Name = T2.Continent INNER JOIN country AS T3 ON T3.Code = T2.Country GROUP BY T3.Name HAVING COUNT(T3.Name) > 1

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start from `continent` and link each continent to its country entries in `encompasses`: `FROM continent AS T1 INNER JOIN encompasses AS T2 ON T1.Name = T2.Continent`.

prefix_hints.sol_3: I group the records by manager so each manager's awards can be counted: `FROM manager_award AS T2 JOIN player AS T1 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id GROUP BY T2.player_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I sort the managers by their award count in descending order and keep the top one: `FROM manager_award AS T2 JOIN player AS T1 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id GROUP BY T2.player_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I project that manager's first name, last name, and id, completing the query: `SELECT T1.name_first ,  T1.name_last ,  T2.player_id FROM player AS T1 JOIN manager_award AS T2 ON T1.player_id  =  T2.player_id GROUP BY T2.player_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1;`.

prefix_hints.sol_2: I continue through the business-category bridge to associate each reviewed business with its categories: `FROM Reviews AS T1 INNER JOIN Business AS T2 ON T1.business_id = T2.business_id INNER JOIN Business_Categories AS T3 ON T2.business_id = T3.business_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I join `Categories` to obtain the category names returned as the requested business names: `FROM Reviews AS T1 INNER JOIN Business AS T2 ON T1.business_id = T2.business_id INNER JOIN Business_Categories AS T3 ON T2.business_id = T3.business_id INNER JOIN Categories AS T4 ON T3.category_id = T4.category_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I keep long reviews and category ids from 1 through 20, then group matching rows by category name: `FROM Reviews AS T1 INNER JOIN Business AS T2 ON T1.business_id = T2.business_id INNER JOIN Business_Categories AS T3 ON T2.business_id = T3.business_id INNER JOIN Categories AS T4 ON T3.category_id = T4.category_id WHERE T1.review_length LIKE 'Long' AND T3.category_id BETWEEN 1 AND 20 GROUP BY T4.category_name`.

ground_truth.answer: SELECT T1.Service_Type_Description , T1.Service_Type_Code FROM Ref_Service_Types AS T1 JOIN Services AS T2 ON T1.Service_Type_Code  =  T2.Service_Type_Code GROUP BY T1.Service_Type_Code ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.sol_1: Service type details and individual services are stored separately, so I join them on the service type code: `FROM Ref_Service_Types AS T1 JOIN Services AS T2 ON T1.Service_Type_Code  =  T2.Service_Type_Code`.

prefix_hints.sol_3: I order the service type groups by their row counts in descending order, placing the most frequently performed type first: `FROM Ref_Service_Types AS T1 JOIN Services AS T2 ON T1.Service_Type_Code  =  T2.Service_Type_Code GROUP BY T1.Service_Type_Code ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I retain only that first, most frequent service type: `FROM Ref_Service_Types AS T1 JOIN Services AS T2 ON T1.Service_Type_Code  =  T2.Service_Type_Code GROUP BY T1.Service_Type_Code ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC LIMIT 1`.

Question:
Please list the bowling skills of all the players from Australia.

Evidence:
Australia refers to Country_Name = 'Australia'
ground_truth.answer: SELECT T2.Bowling_Skill FROM Player AS T1 INNER JOIN Bowling_Style AS T2 ON T1.Bowling_skill = T2.Bowling_Id INNER JOIN Country AS T3 ON T1.Country_Name = T3.Country_Id WHERE T3.Country_Name = 'Australia' GROUP BY T2.Bowling_Skill

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start with players and join their bowling-style ids to the corresponding bowling skills: `FROM Player AS T1 INNER JOIN Bowling_Style AS T2 ON T1.Bowling_skill = T2.Bowling_Id`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join each player to the country table so the player's country name is available: `FROM Player AS T1 INNER JOIN Bowling_Style AS T2 ON T1.Bowling_skill = T2.Bowling_Id INNER JOIN Country AS T3 ON T1.Country_Name = T3.Country_Id`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I restrict the players to those whose country is Australia: `FROM Player AS T1 INNER JOIN Bowling_Style AS T2 ON T1.Bowling_skill = T2.Bowling_Id INNER JOIN Country AS T3 ON T1.Country_Name = T3.Country_Id WHERE T3.Country_Name = 'Australia'`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I group by bowling skill so each skill appears once in the result: `FROM Player AS T1 INNER JOIN Bowling_Style AS T2 ON T1.Bowling_skill = T2.Bowling_Id INNER JOIN Country AS T3 ON T1.Country_Name = T3.Country_Id WHERE T3.Country_Name = 'Australia' GROUP BY T2.Bowling_Skill`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I select the grouped bowling skills to complete the query: `SELECT T2.Bowling_Skill FROM Player AS T1 INNER JOIN Bowling_Style AS T2 ON T1.Bowling_skill = T2.Bowling_Id INNER JOIN Country AS T3 ON T1.Country_Name = T3.Country_Id WHERE T3.Country_Name = 'Australia' GROUP BY T2.Bowling_Skill`.

Question:
Based on the lastet payrate of each employee, calculate the average hourly payrate for each department.

Evidence:
latest payrate refers to max(RateChangeDate); average hourly payrate = divide(sum(Rate), count(BusinessEntityID)) for each DepartmentID
ground_truth.answer: SELECT AVG(T1.Rate) FROM EmployeePayHistory AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeeDepartmentHistory AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID INNER JOIN Department AS T3 ON T2.DepartmentID = T3.DepartmentID WHERE T1.RateChangeDate = ( SELECT MAX(T1.RateChangeDate) FROM EmployeePayHistory AS T1 INNER JOIN Department AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.DepartmentID )

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start from employee pay history, where each employee’s rates and rate-change dates are recorded: `FROM EmployeePayHistory AS T1`.

prefix_hints.sol_3: I keep the records belonging to the Boston Red Stockings: `FROM home_game AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id_br WHERE T2.name = 'Boston Red Stockings'`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I restrict those home-game records to the inclusive period from 1990 through 2000: `FROM home_game AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id_br WHERE T2.name = 'Boston Red Stockings' AND T1.year BETWEEN 1990 AND 2000`.

Question:
For the document Control Assistant who was hired on 2009/1/22, what is the percentage of private documents did he/she have?

Evidence:
Document Control Assistant refers  to the  JobTitle = 'Document Control Assistant'; hired on 2009/1/22 means the person's hiring date is HireDate = '2009-01-22'; private documents indicate that DocumentSummary is null; DIVIDE(COUNT(DocumentSummary is null), COUNT(DocumentSummary))*100
ground_truth.answer: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T1.DocumentSummary IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) / COUNT(T1.DocumentSummary) FROM Document AS T1 INNER JOIN Employee AS T2 ON T1.Owner = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T2.JobTitle = 'Document Control Assistant' AND T2.HireDate = '2009-01-22'

prefix_hints.sol_2: I link each document owner to the corresponding employee: `FROM Document AS T1 INNER JOIN Employee AS T2 ON T1.Owner = T2.BusinessEntityID`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I restrict the owner to the Document Control Assistant hired on 2009-01-22: `FROM Document AS T1 INNER JOIN Employee AS T2 ON T1.Owner = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T2.JobTitle = 'Document Control Assistant' AND T2.HireDate = '2009-01-22'`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I form the numerator by conditionally counting documents with a non-null summary and cast that count to REAL: `SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T1.DocumentSummary IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) FROM Document AS T1 INNER JOIN Employee AS T2 ON T1.Owner = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T2.JobTitle = 'Document Control Assistant' AND T2.HireDate = '2009-01-22'`.

lap record means the fastest time recorded which refers to time
ground_truth.answer: WITH fastest_lap_times AS ( SELECT T1.raceId, T1.FastestLapTime, (CAST(SUBSTR(T1.FastestLapTime, 1, INSTR(T1.FastestLapTime, ':') - 1) AS REAL) * 60) + (CAST(SUBSTR(T1.FastestLapTime, INSTR(T1.FastestLapTime, ':') + 1, INSTR(T1.FastestLapTime, '.') - INSTR(T1.FastestLapTime, ':') - 1) AS REAL)) + (CAST(SUBSTR(T1.FastestLapTime, INSTR(T1.FastestLapTime, '.') + 1) AS REAL) / 1000) as time_in_seconds FROM results AS T1 WHERE T1.FastestLapTime IS NOT NULL ) SELECT T2.name FROM races AS T2 INNER JOIN circuits AS T3 on T2.circuitId = T3.circuitId INNER JOIN results AS T1 on T2.raceId = T1.raceId INNER JOIN ( SELECT MIN(fastest_lap_times.time_in_seconds) as min_time_in_seconds FROM fastest_lap_times INNER JOIN races AS T2 on fastest_lap_times.raceId = T2.raceId INNER JOIN circuits AS T3 on T2.circuitId = T3.circuitId WHERE T2.name = 'Austrian Grand Prix') AS T4 ON (CAST(SUBSTR(T1.FastestLapTime, 1, INSTR(T1.FastestLapTime, ':') - 1) AS REAL) * 60) + (CAST(SUBSTR(T1.FastestLapTime, INSTR(T1.FastestLapTime, ':') + 1, INSTR(T1.FastestLapTime, '.') - INSTR(T1.FastestLapTime, ':') - 1) AS REAL)) + (CAST(SUBSTR(T1.FastestLapTime, INSTR(T1.FastestLapTime, '.') + 1) AS REAL) / 1000) = T4.min_time_in_seconds WHERE T2.name = 'Austrian Grand Prix'

ground_truth.answer: SELECT T1.Actual_Delivery_Date FROM Customer_Orders AS T1 JOIN ORDER_ITEMS AS T2 ON T1.Order_ID  =  T2.Order_ID WHERE T2.Order_Quantity  =  1

prefix_hints.sol_2: I join `ORDER_ITEMS` on the shared order ID so I can associate each order with its quantity: `FROM Customer_Orders AS T1 JOIN ORDER_ITEMS AS T2 ON T1.Order_ID = T2.Order_ID`.

ground_truth.answer: SELECT T1.name_first ,  T1.name_last ,  T2.player_id FROM player AS T1 JOIN manager_award AS T2 ON T1.player_id  =  T2.player_id GROUP BY T2.player_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1;

prefix_hints.sol_1: I link each manager award to the corresponding player record so the manager’s name is available: `FROM player AS T1 JOIN manager_award AS T2 ON T1.player_id  =  T2.player_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I group the joined award records by manager id so each manager’s awards can be counted: `FROM player AS T1 JOIN manager_award AS T2 ON T1.player_id  =  T2.player_id GROUP BY T2.player_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I order the manager groups by their award counts in descending order, placing the manager with the most awards first: `FROM player AS T1 JOIN manager_award AS T2 ON T1.player_id  =  T2.player_id GROUP BY T2.player_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I keep only the first manager in that ranking: `FROM player AS T1 JOIN manager_award AS T2 ON T1.player_id  =  T2.player_id GROUP BY T2.player_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I project that manager’s first name, last name, and player id to complete the query: `SELECT T1.name_first ,  T1.name_last ,  T2.player_id FROM player AS T1 JOIN manager_award AS T2 ON T1.player_id  =  T2.player_id GROUP BY T2.player_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1;`.

Question:
What is the position of the employee with the 10th highest salary? Indicate his/her salary amount and his/her full name.

Evidence:
salary and Rate are synonyms; full name = FirstName+MiddleName+LastName;
ground_truth.answer: SELECT T2.JobTitle, T1.Rate, T3.FirstName, T3.MiddleName, T3.LastName FROM EmployeePayHistory AS T1 INNER JOIN Employee AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID INNER JOIN Person AS T3 ON T2.BusinessEntityID = T3.BusinessEntityID ORDER BY T1.Rate DESC LIMIT 9, 1

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start from `EmployeePayHistory`, where each employee’s salary amount is stored in `Rate`: `FROM EmployeePayHistory AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join `Employee` on the business entity id to obtain the employee’s position from `JobTitle`: `FROM EmployeePayHistory AS T1 INNER JOIN Employee AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I then join `Person` on the same employee identifier and project the position, salary, and the three components of the full name: `SELECT T2.JobTitle, T1.Rate, T3.FirstName, T3.MiddleName, T3.LastName FROM EmployeePayHistory AS T1 INNER JOIN Employee AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID INNER JOIN Person AS T3 ON T2.BusinessEntityID = T3.BusinessEntityID`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I sort the records by salary in descending order so the highest-paid employee appears first: `SELECT T2.JobTitle, T1.Rate, T3.FirstName, T3.MiddleName, T3.LastName FROM EmployeePayHistory AS T1 INNER JOIN Employee AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID INNER JOIN Person AS T3 ON T2.BusinessEntityID = T3.BusinessEntityID ORDER BY T1.Rate DESC`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I skip the first nine salary records and return the next one, which is the employee with the 10th highest salary: `SELECT T2.JobTitle, T1.Rate, T3.FirstName, T3.MiddleName, T3.LastName FROM EmployeePayHistory AS T1 INNER JOIN Employee AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID INNER JOIN Person AS T3 ON T2.BusinessEntityID = T3.BusinessEntityID ORDER BY T1.Rate DESC LIMIT 9, 1`.

Question:
How many times was the budget in Advertisement for "Yearly Kickoff" meeting more than "October Meeting"?

Evidence:
budget in Advertisement refer to category = 'Advertisement' in the budget table; DIVIDE(SUM(amount when event_name = 'Yearly Kickoff'), SUM(amount when event_name = 'October Meeting'))
ground_truth.answer: SELECT CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN T2.event_name = 'Yearly Kickoff' THEN T1.amount ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) / SUM(CASE WHEN T2.event_name = 'October Meeting' THEN T1.amount ELSE 0 END) FROM budget AS T1 INNER JOIN event AS T2 ON T1.link_to_event = T2.event_id WHERE T1.category = 'Advertisement' AND T2.type = 'Meeting'

Question:
Who are the employees that submitted resume to Human Resource Department and got hired? State the last name.

Evidence:
employees that submitted resume to Human Resource Department and got hired refers to BusinessEntittyID NOT null;
ground_truth.answer: SELECT T3.LastName FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN JobCandidate AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID INNER JOIN Person AS T3 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T3.BusinessEntityID WHERE T1.BusinessEntityID IN (212, 274)

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start with the hired employees recorded in `Employee`: `FROM Employee AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I link each employee to the submitted resume in `JobCandidate` through the shared business entity id: `FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN JobCandidate AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I join `Person` on that same id so the employee's last name is available: `FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN JobCandidate AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID INNER JOIN Person AS T3 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T3.BusinessEntityID`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I restrict the result to the identified Human Resources candidates with business entity ids 212 and 274: `FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN JobCandidate AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID INNER JOIN Person AS T3 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T3.BusinessEntityID WHERE T1.BusinessEntityID IN (212, 274)`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I return their last names from `Person`: `SELECT T3.LastName FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN JobCandidate AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID INNER JOIN Person AS T3 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T3.BusinessEntityID WHERE T1.BusinessEntityID IN (212, 274)`.

Show the names of journalists and the number of events they reported.
ground_truth.answer: SELECT T3.Name ,  COUNT(*) FROM news_report AS T1 JOIN event AS T2 ON T1.Event_ID  =  T2.Event_ID JOIN journalist AS T3 ON T1.journalist_ID  =  T3.journalist_ID GROUP BY T3.Name

prefix_hints.sol_3: I then join each report to its journalist so the journalist's name is available: `FROM news_report AS T1 JOIN event AS T2 ON T1.Event_ID = T2.Event_ID JOIN journalist AS T3 ON T1.journalist_ID = T3.journalist_ID`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I group the joined report rows by journalist name so the events can be counted for each journalist: `FROM news_report AS T1 JOIN event AS T2 ON T1.Event_ID = T2.Event_ID JOIN journalist AS T3 ON T1.journalist_ID = T3.journalist_ID GROUP BY T3.Name`.

prefix_hints.sol_2: I join each cast record to its actor so I can check the actor's nationality and count the actor's name: `FROM CAST AS t2 JOIN actor AS t1 ON t2.aid = t1.aid`.

Question:
Name the goalies with the most seasons played. State the average time he played for each season.

Evidence:
most seasons played refers to MAX(COUNT(playerID)); average time he played for each season refers to DIVIDE(SUM(T2.Min),COUNT(T2.playerID))
ground_truth.answer: SELECT T1.firstName, T1.lastName, T2.year, AVG(T2.Min) FROM Master AS T1 INNER JOIN Goalies AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID WHERE T1.playerID = ( SELECT playerID FROM Goalies GROUP BY playerID ORDER BY COUNT(playerID) DESC LIMIT 1 ) GROUP BY T1.firstName, T1.lastName, T2.year

prefix_hints.sol_1: I link each goalie record to the player's name through the shared player ID: `FROM Master AS T1 INNER JOIN Goalies AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I identify the goalie with the greatest number of season records by grouping the goalie rows, sorting their counts descending, and taking the first player: `FROM Master AS T1 INNER JOIN Goalies AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID WHERE T1.playerID = ( SELECT playerID FROM Goalies GROUP BY playerID ORDER BY COUNT(playerID) DESC LIMIT 1 )`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I group that goalie's records by name and season so the playing time can be averaged separately for each year: `FROM Master AS T1 INNER JOIN Goalies AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID WHERE T1.playerID = ( SELECT playerID FROM Goalies GROUP BY playerID ORDER BY COUNT(playerID) DESC LIMIT 1 ) GROUP BY T1.firstName, T1.lastName, T2.year`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I project the goalie's name, season, and average minutes played for that season: `SELECT T1.firstName, T1.lastName, T2.year, AVG(T2.Min) FROM Master AS T1 INNER JOIN Goalies AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID WHERE T1.playerID = ( SELECT playerID FROM Goalies GROUP BY playerID ORDER BY COUNT(playerID) DESC LIMIT 1 ) GROUP BY T1.firstName, T1.lastName, T2.year`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: This completes the query for the goalie with the most season records and his average playing time in each season: `SELECT T1.firstName, T1.lastName, T2.year, AVG(T2.Min) FROM Master AS T1 INNER JOIN Goalies AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID WHERE T1.playerID = ( SELECT playerID FROM Goalies GROUP BY playerID ORDER BY COUNT(playerID) DESC LIMIT 1 ) GROUP BY T1.firstName, T1.lastName, T2.year`.

prefix_hints.sol_1: Attendance records are in `home_game`, so I start from that table and join `team` to obtain the team rank: `FROM home_game AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id  =  T2.team_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I restrict the home-game records to 2014: `FROM home_game AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id  =  T2.team_id WHERE T1.year  =  2014`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I group the records by team so I can calculate each team's average attendance: `FROM home_game AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id  =  T2.team_id WHERE T1.year  =  2014 GROUP BY T1.team_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I sort the teams by average attendance in descending order and retain the highest one: `FROM home_game AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id  =  T2.team_id WHERE T1.year  =  2014 GROUP BY T1.team_id ORDER BY avg(T1.attendance) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I project the selected team's id and rank, completing the query: `SELECT T2.team_id ,  T2.rank FROM home_game AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id  =  T2.team_id WHERE T1.year  =  2014 GROUP BY T1.team_id ORDER BY avg(T1.attendance) DESC LIMIT 1;`.

prefix_hints.sol_3: I group the joined records by student so each group represents all advisors assigned to one student: `FROM student AS T1 JOIN advisor AS T2 ON T1.id = T2.s_id GROUP BY T2.s_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I retain student groups containing more than one advisor record: `FROM student AS T1 JOIN advisor AS T2 ON T1.id = T2.s_id GROUP BY T2.s_id HAVING count(*) > 1`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I return the names of those qualifying students: `SELECT T1.name FROM student AS T1 JOIN advisor AS T2 ON T1.id  =  T2.s_id GROUP BY T2.s_id HAVING count(*)  >  1`.

ground_truth.answer: SELECT t1.player_name FROM Player AS t1 INNER JOIN Player_Attributes AS t2 ON t1.player_api_id = t2.player_api_id WHERE t1.height > 180 GROUP BY t1.id ORDER BY CAST(SUM(t2.heading_accuracy) AS REAL) / COUNT(t2.`player_fifa_api_id`) DESC LIMIT 10

prefix_hints.sol_2: I retain players whose heights are above 180: `FROM Player AS t1 INNER JOIN Player_Attributes AS t2 ON t1.player_api_id = t2.player_api_id WHERE t1.height > 180`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I group the attribute records by player so the average can be calculated for each player: `FROM Player AS t1 INNER JOIN Player_Attributes AS t2 ON t1.player_api_id = t2.player_api_id WHERE t1.height > 180 GROUP BY t1.id`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I order the players descending by heading accuracy sum divided by the attribute-record count, casting the sum to REAL for non-integer division: `FROM Player AS t1 INNER JOIN Player_Attributes AS t2 ON t1.player_api_id = t2.player_api_id WHERE t1.height > 180 GROUP BY t1.id ORDER BY CAST(SUM(t2.heading_accuracy) AS REAL) / COUNT(t2.\`player_fifa_api_id\`) DESC`.

Question:

ground_truth.answer: SELECT name FROM patient EXCEPT SELECT T1.name FROM patient AS T1 JOIN Prescribes AS T2 ON T2.Patient  =  T1.SSN JOIN Medication AS T3 ON T2.Medication  =  T3.Code WHERE T3.name  =  'Procrastin-X'

ground_truth.answer: SELECT T1.pos, T2.award, T1.nameGiven, T1.lastName FROM Master AS T1 INNER JOIN AwardsCoaches AS T2 ON T2.coachID = T1.coachID GROUP BY T1.pos, T2.award, T1.nameGiven, T1.lastName ORDER BY COUNT(T2.award) LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start from `Master`, which provides the position and player name fields: `FROM Master AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I connect each person to their coaching awards through the shared coach identifier: `FROM Master AS T1 INNER JOIN AwardsCoaches AS T2 ON T2.coachID = T1.coachID`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I group the joined records by position, award, and the two player-name fields so each combination has an award count: `FROM Master AS T1 INNER JOIN AwardsCoaches AS T2 ON T2.coachID = T1.coachID GROUP BY T1.pos, T2.award, T1.nameGiven, T1.lastName`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I order these groups by their award count: `FROM Master AS T1 INNER JOIN AwardsCoaches AS T2 ON T2.coachID = T1.coachID GROUP BY T1.pos, T2.award, T1.nameGiven, T1.lastName ORDER BY COUNT(T2.award)`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I return the position, award name, given name, and last name from the first ordered group: `SELECT T1.pos, T2.award, T1.nameGiven, T1.lastName FROM Master AS T1 INNER JOIN AwardsCoaches AS T2 ON T2.coachID = T1.coachID GROUP BY T1.pos, T2.award, T1.nameGiven, T1.lastName ORDER BY COUNT(T2.award) LIMIT 1`.

Which customer has the highest subtotal amount of sales orders whose assigned to the salesperson with the highest bonus?

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start from the sales order records, which contain each customer, assigned salesperson, and subtotal: `FROM SalesOrderHeader AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join the assigned salesperson through the salesperson's business entity id: `FROM SalesOrderHeader AS T1 INNER JOIN SalesPerson AS T2 ON T1.SalesPersonID = T2.BusinessEntityID`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I project the customer identifier from each matched sales order: `SELECT T1.CustomerID FROM SalesOrderHeader AS T1 INNER JOIN SalesPerson AS T2 ON T1.SalesPersonID = T2.BusinessEntityID`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I sort the orders by subtotal in descending order so the highest subtotal comes first: `SELECT T1.CustomerID FROM SalesOrderHeader AS T1 INNER JOIN SalesPerson AS T2 ON T1.SalesPersonID = T2.BusinessEntityID ORDER BY T1.SubTotal DESC`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I retain the first row to return the customer associated with that highest subtotal: `SELECT T1.CustomerID FROM SalesOrderHeader AS T1 INNER JOIN SalesPerson AS T2 ON T1.SalesPersonID = T2.BusinessEntityID ORDER BY T1.SubTotal DESC LIMIT 1`.

Question:
Find the names of the customers who have order status both "On Road" and "Shipped".
ground_truth.answer: SELECT T1.customer_name FROM customers AS T1 JOIN orders AS T2 ON T1.customer_id = T2.customer_id WHERE T2.order_status = "On Road" INTERSECT SELECT T1.customer_name FROM customers AS T1 JOIN orders AS T2 ON T1.customer_id = T2.customer_id WHERE T2.order_status = "Shipped"

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start with customer names and join each customer to their orders through the shared customer id: `SELECT T1.customer_name FROM customers AS T1 JOIN orders AS T2 ON T1.customer_id = T2.customer_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I restrict this first customer set to orders whose status is "On Road": `SELECT T1.customer_name FROM customers AS T1 JOIN orders AS T2 ON T1.customer_id = T2.customer_id WHERE T2.order_status = "On Road"`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: To require the other status as well, I intersect the first set with a second selection of customer names: `SELECT T1.customer_name FROM customers AS T1 JOIN orders AS T2 ON T1.customer_id = T2.customer_id WHERE T2.order_status = "On Road" INTERSECT SELECT T1.customer_name FROM customers AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I join the customers in the second selection to their orders on customer id: `SELECT T1.customer_name FROM customers AS T1 JOIN orders AS T2 ON T1.customer_id = T2.customer_id WHERE T2.order_status = "On Road" INTERSECT SELECT T1.customer_name FROM customers AS T1 JOIN orders AS T2 ON T1.customer_id = T2.customer_id`.

Question:
List all deceased goalies by last name. List the season where he had the most time played.

Evidence:
deceased refers to deathYear; most time played refers to MAX(Min)
ground_truth.answer: SELECT T1.playerID, T2.year, Min FROM Master AS T1 INNER JOIN Goalies AS T2 ON T2.playerID = T1.playerID WHERE T1.deathYear IS NOT NULL ORDER BY T2.Min DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.sol_4: I take the first row after that ordering to identify the season with the most time played: `FROM Master AS T1 INNER JOIN Goalies AS T2 ON T2.playerID = T1.playerID WHERE T1.deathYear IS NOT NULL ORDER BY T2.Min DESC LIMIT 1`.

ground_truth.answer: SELECT T1.Name FROM country AS T1 INNER JOIN economy AS T2 ON T1.Code = T2.Country WHERE T2.Inflation IS NOT NULL ORDER BY T2.Inflation ASC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.sol_3: I sort the remaining countries by inflation from lowest to highest: `FROM country AS T1 INNER JOIN economy AS T2 ON T1.Code = T2.Country WHERE T2.Inflation IS NOT NULL ORDER BY T2.Inflation ASC`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: The first row in that ordering is the country with the lowest inflation, so I limit the result to one row: `FROM country AS T1 INNER JOIN economy AS T2 ON T1.Code = T2.Country WHERE T2.Inflation IS NOT NULL ORDER BY T2.Inflation ASC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I return that country's name: `SELECT T1.Name FROM country AS T1 INNER JOIN economy AS T2 ON T1.Code = T2.Country WHERE T2.Inflation IS NOT NULL ORDER BY T2.Inflation ASC LIMIT 1`.

prefix_hints.sol_4: I use this country value to restrict the geographic mountain records: `FROM geo_mountain WHERE Country = ( SELECT Country FROM economy ORDER BY Inflation ASC LIMIT 1 )`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I return the mountain names from those matching records: `SELECT Mountain FROM geo_mountain WHERE Country = ( SELECT Country FROM economy ORDER BY Inflation ASC LIMIT 1 )`.

Question:
What is the average vacation hours taken by Sales person?

Evidence:
Store Contact refers PersonType = 'SC'; AVG(VacationHours
ground_truth.answer: SELECT CAST(SUM(T1.VacationHours) AS REAL) / COUNT(T1.BusinessEntityID) FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T2.PersonType = 'SP'

prefix_hints.sol_1: Vacation hours are recorded for employees, so I start from the `Employee` table: `FROM Employee AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join each employee to their person record so I can identify the person type: `FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I keep the salespeople identified by `PersonType = 'SP'`: `FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T2.PersonType = 'SP'`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I compute their average by dividing the vacation-hour sum, cast to REAL, by the salesperson count: `SELECT CAST(SUM(T1.VacationHours) AS REAL) / COUNT(T1.BusinessEntityID) FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T2.PersonType = 'SP'`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: This completes the average vacation-hours query: `SELECT CAST(SUM(T1.VacationHours) AS REAL) / COUNT(T1.BusinessEntityID) FROM Employee AS T1 INNER JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.BusinessEntityID = T2.BusinessEntityID WHERE T2.PersonType = 'SP'`.

ground_truth.answer: SELECT SUM(T1.L), SUM(T2.A) FROM Teams AS T1 INNER JOIN Scoring AS T2 ON T1.tmID = T2.tmID AND T1.year = T2.year WHERE T1.tmID = 'BOS' AND T1.year = 2010

prefix_hints.sol_3: I restrict the joined records to team BOS: `FROM Teams AS T1 INNER JOIN Scoring AS T2 ON T1.tmID = T2.tmID AND T1.year = T2.year WHERE T1.tmID = 'BOS'`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I further restrict the result to the 2010 season: `FROM Teams AS T1 INNER JOIN Scoring AS T2 ON T1.tmID = T2.tmID AND T1.year = T2.year WHERE T1.tmID = 'BOS' AND T1.year = 2010`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I sum the team losses and the players' assists for the matched records: `SELECT SUM(T1.L), SUM(T2.A) FROM Teams AS T1 INNER JOIN Scoring AS T2 ON T1.tmID = T2.tmID AND T1.year = T2.year WHERE T1.tmID = 'BOS' AND T1.year = 2010`.

Question:
Give the name of the league had the most matches end as draw in the 2016 season?

Evidence:
most matches end as draw refers to MAX(SUM(home_team_goal = away_team_goal)); 2016 season refers to season = '2015/2016';
ground_truth.answer: SELECT t2.name FROM Match AS t1 INNER JOIN League AS t2 ON t1.league_id = t2.id WHERE t1.season = '2015/2016' AND t1.home_team_goal = t1.away_team_goal GROUP BY t2.name ORDER BY COUNT(t1.id) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.sol_1: Match records identify their leagues by `league_id`, so I join `Match` to `League` to make the league name available: `FROM Match AS t1 INNER JOIN League AS t2 ON t1.league_id = t2.id`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I restrict the matches to the season represented by `2015/2016`: `FROM Match AS t1 INNER JOIN League AS t2 ON t1.league_id = t2.id WHERE t1.season = '2015/2016'`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I then keep only draws, where the home and away goal totals are equal: `FROM Match AS t1 INNER JOIN League AS t2 ON t1.league_id = t2.id WHERE t1.season = '2015/2016' AND t1.home_team_goal = t1.away_team_goal`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I group the draws by league name and rank the leagues by their match counts in descending order, keeping the top one: `FROM Match AS t1 INNER JOIN League AS t2 ON t1.league_id = t2.id WHERE t1.season = '2015/2016' AND t1.home_team_goal = t1.away_team_goal GROUP BY t2.name ORDER BY COUNT(t1.id) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: Finally, I return the name of the league with the highest draw count: `SELECT t2.name FROM Match AS t1 INNER JOIN League AS t2 ON t1.league_id = t2.id WHERE t1.season = '2015/2016' AND t1.home_team_goal = t1.away_team_goal GROUP BY t2.name ORDER BY COUNT(t1.id) DESC LIMIT 1`.

Question:
Indicate the name of the actors of the films rated as 'Parents Strongly Precautioned' with the highest replacement cost.

Evidence:
name refers to first_name, last_name; Parents Strongly Precautioned' refers to rating = 'PG-13'; 
highest replacement cost refers to MAX(replacement_cost)
ground_truth.answer: SELECT T1.first_name, T1.last_name FROM actor AS T1 INNER JOIN film_actor AS T2 ON T1.actor_id = T2.actor_id INNER JOIN film AS T3 ON T2.film_id = T3.film_id WHERE T3.rating = 'PG-13' ORDER BY T3.replacement_cost DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start with actors and link them to their film assignments through the shared actor id: `FROM actor AS T1 INNER JOIN film_actor AS T2 ON T1.actor_id = T2.actor_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join those assignments to `film` so each actor is associated with the film's rating and replacement cost: `FROM actor AS T1 INNER JOIN film_actor AS T2 ON T1.actor_id = T2.actor_id INNER JOIN film AS T3 ON T2.film_id = T3.film_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I restrict the films to the Parents Strongly Cautioned rating, represented by `PG-13`: `FROM actor AS T1 INNER JOIN film_actor AS T2 ON T1.actor_id = T2.actor_id INNER JOIN film AS T3 ON T2.film_id = T3.film_id WHERE T3.rating = 'PG-13'`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I sort the qualifying films by replacement cost in descending order so the highest cost comes first: `FROM actor AS T1 INNER JOIN film_actor AS T2 ON T1.actor_id = T2.actor_id INNER JOIN film AS T3 ON T2.film_id = T3.film_id WHERE T3.rating = 'PG-13' ORDER BY T3.replacement_cost DESC`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I select the actor's first and last names and retain the first row from that ordering: `SELECT T1.first_name, T1.last_name FROM actor AS T1 INNER JOIN film_actor AS T2 ON T1.actor_id = T2.actor_id INNER JOIN film AS T3 ON T2.film_id = T3.film_id WHERE T3.rating = 'PG-13' ORDER BY T3.replacement_cost DESC LIMIT 1`.

Question:

Evidence:
Information Service is a name of department;
ground_truth.answer: SELECT COUNT(T2.BusinessEntityID) FROM Department AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeeDepartmentHistory AS T2 ON T1.DepartmentID = T2.DepartmentID INNER JOIN Shift AS T3 ON T2.ShiftId = T3.ShiftId WHERE T1.Name = 'Information Services' AND T3.Name = 'Evening'

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start with `Department` so I can identify the department by name: `FROM Department AS T1`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join the employee department history on the department id to get the employees assigned there: `FROM Department AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeeDepartmentHistory AS T2 ON T1.DepartmentID = T2.DepartmentID`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I join `Shift` through the history record so each assignment can be matched to its shift name: `FROM Department AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeeDepartmentHistory AS T2 ON T1.DepartmentID = T2.DepartmentID INNER JOIN Shift AS T3 ON T2.ShiftId = T3.ShiftId`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I restrict the assignments to the Information Services department and the Evening shift: `FROM Department AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeeDepartmentHistory AS T2 ON T1.DepartmentID = T2.DepartmentID INNER JOIN Shift AS T3 ON T2.ShiftId = T3.ShiftId WHERE T1.Name = 'Information Services' AND T3.Name = 'Evening'`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I count the employee identifiers in the matching history records, completing the query: `SELECT COUNT(T2.BusinessEntityID) FROM Department AS T1 INNER JOIN EmployeeDepartmentHistory AS T2 ON T1.DepartmentID = T2.DepartmentID INNER JOIN Shift AS T3 ON T2.ShiftId = T3.ShiftId WHERE T1.Name = 'Information Services' AND T3.Name = 'Evening'`.

closed events refers to event_name where status = 'Closed'; highest spend-to budget ratio refers to MAX(DIVIDE(spent, amount))
ground_truth.answer: SELECT T2.event_name FROM budget AS T1 INNER JOIN event AS T2 ON T1.link_to_event = T2.event_id WHERE T2.status = 'Closed' ORDER BY T1.spent / T1.amount DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.sol_1: I link each budget record to its event so I can compare spending figures while identifying the event: `FROM budget AS T1 INNER JOIN event AS T2 ON T1.link_to_event = T2.event_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I restrict the joined records to events whose status is Closed: `FROM budget AS T1 INNER JOIN event AS T2 ON T1.link_to_event = T2.event_id WHERE T2.status = 'Closed'`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I rank the closed events by spent divided by budget amount in descending order, placing the highest ratio first: `FROM budget AS T1 INNER JOIN event AS T2 ON T1.link_to_event = T2.event_id WHERE T2.status = 'Closed' ORDER BY T1.spent / T1.amount DESC`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I project the event name from that ranking: `SELECT T2.event_name FROM budget AS T1 INNER JOIN event AS T2 ON T1.link_to_event = T2.event_id WHERE T2.status = 'Closed' ORDER BY T1.spent / T1.amount DESC`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I take only the first ranked event to return the one with the highest spend-to-budget ratio: `SELECT T2.event_name FROM budget AS T1 INNER JOIN event AS T2 ON T1.link_to_event = T2.event_id WHERE T2.status = 'Closed' ORDER BY T1.spent / T1.amount DESC LIMIT 1`.

Question:
What are the first, middle, and last names for everybody enrolled in a Bachelors program?
ground_truth.answer: SELECT DISTINCT T1.first_name ,  T1.middle_name ,  T1.last_name FROM Students AS T1 JOIN Student_Enrolment AS T2 ON T1.student_id  =  T2.student_id JOIN Degree_Programs AS T3 ON T2.degree_program_id  =  T3.degree_program_id WHERE T3.degree_summary_name  =  'Bachelor'

prefix_hints.sol_1: I start with students and connect each student to their enrollment records by student id: `FROM Students AS T1 JOIN Student_Enrolment AS T2 ON T1.student_id = T2.student_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_2: I join each enrollment to its degree program so the program name is available: `FROM Students AS T1 JOIN Student_Enrolment AS T2 ON T1.student_id = T2.student_id JOIN Degree_Programs AS T3 ON T2.degree_program_id = T3.degree_program_id`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I restrict the rows to enrollments whose degree summary name is Bachelor: `FROM Students AS T1 JOIN Student_Enrolment AS T2 ON T1.student_id = T2.student_id JOIN Degree_Programs AS T3 ON T2.degree_program_id = T3.degree_program_id WHERE T3.degree_summary_name = 'Bachelor'`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I project the first, middle, and last names, using DISTINCT so each enrolled person appears once: `SELECT DISTINCT T1.first_name, T1.middle_name, T1.last_name FROM Students AS T1 JOIN Student_Enrolment AS T2 ON T1.student_id = T2.student_id JOIN Degree_Programs AS T3 ON T2.degree_program_id = T3.degree_program_id WHERE T3.degree_summary_name = 'Bachelor'`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: This completes the query: `SELECT DISTINCT T1.first_name ,  T1.middle_name ,  T1.last_name FROM Students AS T1 JOIN Student_Enrolment AS T2 ON T1.student_id  =  T2.student_id JOIN Degree_Programs AS T3 ON T2.degree_program_id  =  T3.degree_program_id WHERE T3.degree_summary_name  =  'Bachelor'`.

Question:
For the goalie who had the highest defensive success rate in the postseason of 2011, what's his legends ID ?

Evidence:
Post season of 2011 refers to year = ’2011’
defensive success rate refers to (SUBTRACT(1 (DIVIDE(PostGA/PostSA)), *100%)
ground_truth.answer: SELECT T2.legendsID FROM Goalies AS T1 INNER JOIN Master AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID WHERE T1.year = 2011 ORDER BY 1 - CAST(T1.PostGA AS REAL) / T1.PostSA DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.sol_2: I join `Master` by player ID so the goalie's legends ID is available: `FROM Goalies AS T1 INNER JOIN Master AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID`.
prefix_hints.sol_3: I restrict the goalie records to the 2011 season: `FROM Goalies AS T1 INNER JOIN Master AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID WHERE T1.year = 2011`.
prefix_hints.sol_4: I rank the goalies by descending defensive success rate, casting `PostGA` to REAL for the division, and retain the top result: `FROM Goalies AS T1 INNER JOIN Master AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID WHERE T1.year = 2011 ORDER BY 1 - CAST(T1.PostGA AS REAL) / T1.PostSA DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.sol_5: I project the legends ID of that highest-ranked goalie, completing the query: `SELECT T2.legendsID FROM Goalies AS T1 INNER JOIN Master AS T2 ON T1.playerID = T2.playerID WHERE T1.year = 2011 ORDER BY 1 - CAST(T1.PostGA AS REAL) / T1.PostSA DESC LIMIT 1`.
